description: Grape leaf blight causes angular necrotic spots and premature defoliation, reducing canopy function and fruit ripening.
causes: The fungus survives in infected leaves and spreads by rain splash during warm, humid growing conditions.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown angular leaf spots
Gray or tan centers with dark margins
Spots coalescing into blighted tissue
Premature leaf drop and reduced vine vigor
organic_treatment: Remove infected leaves and improve canopy airflow; use labeled copper or sulfur products as preventative protection.
chemical_treatment: Apply a registered grape fungicide such as mancozeb or a labeled strobilurin according to local regulations and resistance guidance.
prevention: Remove fallen leaves, manage canopy density, avoid prolonged leaf wetness, and use tolerant planting material.

description: Late blight is a devastating oomycete disease that affects tomatoes and potatoes worldwide. It can destroy an entire field within days under cool, wet, and humid conditions.
causes: Caused by the fungus-like oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Spores are transported by wind or splashing rain, thriving in 60-70°F (15-21°C) with persistent moisture.
symptoms: Irregular, dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems
White, fuzzy fungal growth on undersides of leaves during humid mornings
Large, firm, dark brown greasy lesions on green fruit
Rapid wilting, browning, and collapse of foliage
organic_treatment: Immediately prune and bag infected foliage (do not compost). Apply copper-based fungicides (Bordeaux mixture or copper octanoate) every 5-7 days. Spray biofungicides containing Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Serenade (Bacillus subtilis).
chemical_treatment: Apply systemic fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or cymoxanil + famoxadone at first sign. Rotate with fluopicolide or mandipropamid to prevent resistance.
prevention: Avoid overhead watering; use drip irrigation. Ensure wide plant spacing for airflow. Plant certified disease-resistant varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Merit, Legend). Destroy cull piles.

description: Early blight is a common fungal disease that attacks leaves, stems, and fruits, primarily starting on older lower foliage and progressing upwards.
causes: Caused by Alternaria solani. The fungus overwinters in crop debris, soil, and solanaceous weeds. Spores spread by wind, rain splashes, and cultivation tools.
symptoms: Circular brown-to-black spots with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellow halos (chlorosis) surrounding the dark leaf spots
Lower leaves wither, die, and drop prematurely (sunscald vulnerability)
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at stem ends of fruits
organic_treatment: Remove lower leaves up to 18 inches from the soil line. Apply neem oil, copper hydroxide, or potassium bicarbonate sprays every 7-10 days. Mulch heavily around plants to prevent soil splash.
chemical_treatment: Spray preventive fungicides like Azoxystrobin, Chlorothalonil, or Pyraclostrobin early in the season before extensive lesions spread.
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops. Stake and trellis plants for maximum sunlight and aeration. Water at the base only.

description: Leaf mold predominantly impacts greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes where relative humidity exceeds 85%, reducing photosynthesis and yield.
causes: Favored by warm temperatures (70-75°F / 21-24°C) and prolonged periods of high humidity (>85% RH). Spores survive in greenhouse structures and seed coats.
symptoms: Pale green to pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with diffuse margins
Olive-green to brown velvety mold carpet on the corresponding undersurface
Leaves curl, turn brown, and drop off
Flower blossoms blighted, causing blossom drop
organic_treatment: Ventilate greenhouses with circulation fans to lower relative humidity below 80%. Apply sulfur dust or copper sulfate. Spray compost tea enriched with beneficial Trichoderma.
chemical_treatment: Treat with triflumizole, azoxystrobin, or cyprodinil + fludioxonil according to label rates during high humidity conditions.
prevention: Keep foliage strictly dry. Increase vent spacing and raise greenhouse heat slightly at dusk to prevent condensation on leaf surfaces.

description: TYLCV is a devastating geminivirus transmitted by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), capable of causing 100% crop loss if infection occurs early.
causes: Vector transmission by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci biotype B and Q. Not seed-transmitted or mechanically transmitted through touch.
symptoms: Severe stunting of young plants and bushy appearance
Leaves cupped upwards with interveinal chlorosis and yellow margins
Marked reduction in leaf size ('little leaf' appearance)
Flower drop and drastic reduction in fruit setting; remaining fruit is small and deformed
organic_treatment: Eradicate whitefly vectors using insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, and neem-derived azadirachtin. Install fine 50-mesh insect netting in greenhouses and yellow sticky traps in fields.
chemical_treatment: Apply systemic insecticides targeting whiteflies (e.g., imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, or cyantraniliprole) early in transplant stages. Rotate modes of action.
prevention: Plant certified TYLCV-resistant hybrids (e.g., Tygress, Skyway, Charger). Eradicate volunteer nightshades and weeds around perimeter.

description: Foliage exhibits vibrant green chlorophyll saturation, robust vascular turgidity, uniform leaf structure, and no signs of bacterial, viral, or fungal pathology.
causes: Optimal soil nutrition, balanced moisture, adequate sunlight, and effective pest management.
symptoms: Vibrant uniform deep-green leaf blade without chlorosis or necrosis
Firm, well-developed stems with healthy trichomes (hairs)
Clean margins without lesions, spots, or curling
Vigorous blossom development and fruit set
organic_treatment: Continue routine organic fertilization (balanced compost, fish emulsion, kelp meal). Maintain 2-3 inches of clean straw mulch.
chemical_treatment: No treatment needed. Maintain preventative integrated pest management (IPM) scouting.
prevention: Consistent drip irrigation, regular calcium supply to prevent blossom end rot, and periodic pruning of ground suckers.

description: A prevalent fungal foliar disease in potato production that causes premature canopy defoliation and tuber dry rot.
causes: Alternaria solani survives in infected crop debris. Favorable conditions include warm temperatures (75-85°F) alternating with wet and dry periods.
symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots showing distinct target-like concentric rings
Spots coalesce causing leaf margins to curl and dry up ('firing')
Tuber infection shows brown, dry, sunken irregular surface lesions with purple cast
Premature vine dying and reduced tuber bulk
organic_treatment: Foliar spray with liquid copper or Bacillus subtilis at weekly intervals. Ensure optimal nitrogen fertility as stressed plants are much more susceptible.
chemical_treatment: Standard protective sprays with Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Pyraclostrobin beginning at canopy closure.
prevention: Destroy volunteer potatoes; practice 3 to 4-year crop rotations; kill potato vines 2 weeks prior to harvest to prevent tuber contamination.

description: Historically responsible for the Irish Potato Famine, late blight remains one of the most destructive agricultural diseases known, capable of rotting entire potato fields in 7-10 days.
causes: Phytophthora infestans oomycete spores carried by cool, damp wind currents. Survives between seasons exclusively in living potato tuber tissue.
symptoms: Irregular dark green to purplish-brown water-soaked lesions expanding rapidly
Faint white cottony mildew under the leaf margin during high humidity
Stem rot turning dark brown and brittle, collapsing stems
Tubers develop granular, reddish-brown dry rot extending inward under skin
organic_treatment: Immediately destroy and bury heavily infected vines. Apply fixed copper sprays before rain events to protect healthy foliage.
chemical_treatment: Immediate application of specific anti-oomycete compounds: mandipropamid, fluopicolide, or dimethomorph combined with a protectant fungicide.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers. Eliminate all cull piles by burying or freezing. Monitor regional late-blight forecast systems.

description: Vigorous potato canopy with rich, crisp emerald leaves, sturdy upright stems, and optimal vegetative growth without pathogen infestation.
causes: Good seed potato quality, adequate hilling, balanced phosphorus-potassium soil profile, and proper moisture control.
symptoms: Lush, uniform green leaf color across top and bottom tiers
No spotting, yellowing margins, or stem darkening
Erect, sturdy vegetative canopy with good turgor
Robust root stolons setting healthy tuber clusters
organic_treatment: Continue balanced organic hilling and compost tea applications.
chemical_treatment: No chemical treatment required.
prevention: Maintain scheduled soil moisture monitoring, hill potatoes every 2-3 weeks, and inspect for Colorado potato beetle.

description: Common rust is an airborne fungal disease of corn characterized by prominent cinnamon-brown pustules across both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
causes: Puccinia sorghi fungal urediniospores blown northward each spring from tropical and subtropical regions. Thrives in moderate temperatures (60-75°F) with high humidity.
symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown powdery pustules (uredinia) scattered on leaves
Pustules rupture through both upper and lower epidermal layers
Pustules darken to brownish-black late in the season (teliospore stage)
Severe infections lead to leaf chlorosis, necrosis, and premature lodging
organic_treatment: Apply sulfur dusts or copper fungicides at the earliest detection of rust flecks. Enhance soil mycorrhizal biology.
chemical_treatment: Foliar fungicides such as azoxystrobin + propiconazole, pyraclostrobin + metconazole, or trifloxystrobin applied at tassel emergence (VT to R1) if pustules are present on ear leaves.
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with high polygenic or monogenic (Rp) resistance genes. Early planting often allows corn to mature before spore loads peak.

description: A devastating foliar fungal disease that causes extensive necrotic cigar-shaped lesions on corn leaves, drastically reducing grain fill.
causes: Overwinters in corn residue. Spores are splashed or windblown onto leaves during moderate temperatures (65-80°F) accompanied by extended 6-12 hour dew periods.
symptoms: Distinct long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (1-6 inches long)
Lesions feature smooth margins and develop dark fungal spore mat in damp weather
Lesions merge, creating broad strips of dead leaf tissue
Stalk weakening and susceptibility to secondary stalk rots
organic_treatment: Crop residue management: shred and shallowly incorporate corn stover to accelerate microbial breakdown. Apply sulfur or biological sprays.
chemical_treatment: Apply triazole or strobilurin fungicides (e.g., Pyraclostrobin, Fluxapyroxad, or Tebuconazole) if disease reaches the leaf below the ear before silking.
prevention: Choose resistant hybrids carrying Ht genes. Implement minimum 1-year crop rotation with soybeans, alfalfa, or oats.

description: Vigorous maize plant displaying deep green, ribbon-like leaves with clean venation, robust brace roots, and pristine ear shoot development.
causes: Balanced nitrogen supply, well-drained loam soil, sufficient thermal units, and pest-free microclimate.
symptoms: Broad, arching deep green leaves with crisp parallel veins
Absence of pustules, striping, or necrotic blotches
Thick, resilient stalk with strong nodal tissue
Healthy tassel shedding pollen and uniform silk emergence
organic_treatment: Maintain side-dressed organic nitrogen (feather meal, blood meal, compost). Ensure deep watering during pollination.
chemical_treatment: None required.
prevention: Maintain soil fertility testing, avoid compaction, scout weekly for corn borers and armyworms.

description: Apple scab is the single most destructive disease of commercial apples, causing dark velvety lesions on leaves and corky blemishes on fruit that ruin market value.
causes: Overwinters in dead fallen leaves on the orchard floor. Spring rains trigger ascospores release, infecting new green tissue when wet for 6-12 hours.
symptoms: Olive-green to velvety brown-black spots with feathered edges on upper leaf surfaces
Leaves become distorted, puckered, curled, and drop prematurely in mid-summer
Fruit develops scabby, corky, cracked dark lesions that deform shape
Twig lesions can develop on young vegetative growth
organic_treatment: Spray lime-sulfur or micronized sulfur at green tip through petal fall. Flail mow and spray orchard floor with 5% urea or compost extract in autumn to decompose fallen leaves.
chemical_treatment: Preventative sterol-inhibitors (myclobutanil, difenoconazole) or strobilurins (kresoxim-methyl, trifloxystrobin) mixed with protectants like captan or mancozeb.
prevention: Prune tree canopies in winter for maximum air and sun penetration. Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Honeycrisp).

description: A fungal disease affecting apple leaves (frogeye leaf spot), branches (cankers), and fruit (black rot), often leading to tree dieback.
causes: Fungus survives in dead wood, fire blight strikes, and mummified apples left on trees. Spores germinate across wide temperatures (60-80°F).
symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots: small purple specks expanding into brown spots with distinct purple margins
Fruit rot begins at calyx as firm brown ring expanding into concentric alternating brown and black bands
Rotting fruit mummifies and stays attached to branches over winter
Sunken, reddish-brown bark cankers with cracked outer margins
organic_treatment: Physically remove and burn all mummified apples and dead twigs during winter dormancy. Apply copper fungicides during early bud break.
chemical_treatment: Captan, Thiophanate-methyl, or Mancozeb sprays timed from pink bud through cover sprays.
prevention: Prune out all dead or damaged wood 6 inches below cankers. Maintain tree vigor with balanced fertilizer; avoid bark injury from equipment.

description: Pristine apple orchard foliage showing glossy green leaves, clean branches, sturdy spur systems, and blemish-free pomes.
causes: Balanced winter pruning, dormant oil sprays, excellent air circulation, and proper orchard floor management.
symptoms: Vibrant glossy green leaves without spots, puckering, or powdery residues
Smooth, intact bark on scaffold branches and fruiting spurs
Vigorous shoot growth (12-18 inches per season)
Uniform fruit development with clean epidermis
organic_treatment: Continue standard dormant organic oil spray in late winter to suppress overwintering insect pests.
chemical_treatment: None required.
prevention: Maintain tree branch training (60-degree scaffold angles), thin fruits to one per cluster, and irrigate during dry spells.

description: One of the most destructive diseases of cultivated grapes in warm, humid climates. Capable of causing 100% loss of berry clusters if unchecked.
causes: Overwinters in mummified berries on the trellis wire and vineyard floor. Fungal ascospores release during warm spring rains.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with dark margins and tiny black dots (pycnidia)
Infected berries turn light brown, soften, shrink, and shrivel into hard black 'mummies'
Black sunken oval cankers on young shoots and tendrils
Complete cluster desiccation
organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all mummified clusters during winter pruning. Apply copper sulfate or sulfur fungicides from bud break through veraison.
chemical_treatment: Apply myclobutanil, tebuconazole, or azoxystrobin beginning at 1-inch shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom.
prevention: Trellis canopy management to maximize leaf exposure to wind and sun. Keep vineyard rows weed-free for airflow.

description: Esca is a complex grapevine trunk disease affecting mature vines, causing characteristic tiger-stripe foliar patterns, fruit spotting, and internal wood decay.
causes: Fungal pathogens enter through pruning wounds and harvest cuts, slowly colonizing the xylem vascular system over several years.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' foliar pattern: interveinal yellowing and browning bordered by chlorotic bands
Berry spotting: tiny dark purple to black speckles ('measles') on green or ripening fruit
Apoplexy: sudden total vine collapse and wilting during hot summer days
Dark brown wood necrosis visible in cross-section of cordons
organic_treatment: Paint pruning cuts with bio-protectant Trichoderma formulations. Prune late in the dormant season when wound healing is rapid.
chemical_treatment: Apply wound protectants containing thiophanate-methyl immediately after pruning cuts. No curative chemical treatment exists for internal wood rot.
prevention: Use clean, certified nursery stock. Avoid making large pruning wounds in wet weather. Mark and rogue severely degraded vines.

description: Lush grapevine canopy with clean palmate leaves, vigorous shoot tips, intact tendrils, and clean developing clusters.
causes: Optimal canopy training (VSP or Scott Henry), balanced vine balance, deficit irrigation, and timely seasonal canopy hedging.
symptoms: Broad, emerald green leaves free of interveinal chlorosis or spotting
Rapidly growing shoot tips with healthy curling tendrils
Clean green canes without necrotic lesions or blistering
Uniform cluster elongation and berry set
organic_treatment: Continue compost mulch along vine rows and leaf-pulling in the fruiting zone for sunlight.
chemical_treatment: None required.
prevention: Scout for leafhoppers and powdery mildew, hedge canopy top to prevent shade crowding.

description: A serious seed-borne and water-splashed bacterial disease causing foliar defoliation and blister-like unmarketable fruit lesions in sweet peppers.
causes: Bacteria multiply rapidly in warm (75-86°F), rainy, and humid weather. Spreads through driving rain, splashing sprinklers, and handling wet plants.
symptoms: Small water-soaked or translucent circular spots on leaves becoming brown with yellow halos
Spots coalesce into large necrotic tears, causing severe leaf drop
Fruit develops raised, rough, wart-like brown scabby blisters
Stem cankers that weaken branch crotches
organic_treatment: Apply copper bactericides mixed with Bacillus subtilis or Serenade Max. Spray actigard (acibenzolar-S-methyl) to induce systemic acquired resistance (SAR).
chemical_treatment: Fixed copper compounds combined with mancozeb (co-spray significantly improves efficacy against copper-tolerant strains).
prevention: Use certified hot-water treated pathogen-free seeds. Never work in pepper fields while foliage is wet. Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2 years.

description: Sturdy bell pepper foliage exhibiting rich dark green color, thick waxy cuticle, symmetrical leaf structure, and vibrant white star-shaped flowers.
causes: Adequate soil temperature (>65°F), consistent moisture, balanced nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium fertility, and integrated pest control.
symptoms: Glossy, deep green oval-lanceolate leaves with smooth margins
Strong main stem and bushy lateral branching
Abundant pristine white floral blossoms with vibrant yellow anthers
Blocky, thick-walled green or ripening bell fruits without blemishes
organic_treatment: Feed with organic fish-seaweed emulsion and maintain soil moisture with clean organic straw mulch.
chemical_treatment: None required.
prevention: Ensure adequate soil calcium to prevent blossom end rot, water at soil level, stake heavy fruiting branches.

description: A rust disease that alternates between apple trees and susceptible juniper hosts, causing foliar spotting and reduced fruit quality.
causes: Windborne spores from infected junipers infect young apple leaves during cool, wet spring weather.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange leaf spots
Orange cup-like structures on leaf undersides
Premature leaf drop
Small or malformed fruit
organic_treatment: Remove nearby infected juniper galls where practical and apply approved sulfur or copper products according to the label.
chemical_treatment: Use labeled fungicides such as myclobutanil or tebuconazole during the spring infection period, rotating modes of action.
prevention: Plant resistant apple cultivars and separate apple orchards from alternate juniper hosts.

description: Healthy blueberry foliage with uniform green leaves, active growth, and no visible disease lesions or abnormal discoloration.
causes: Appropriate acidic soil, balanced nutrition, adequate moisture, and good air circulation support healthy growth.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves
Firm stems and healthy new growth
No spots, blight, or wilt
Normal flowering and fruit development
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain compost-based nutrition and mulch without covering the crown.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; continue routine scouting and use products only for a confirmed pest or disease.
prevention: Maintain acidic soil near the crop requirement, drip irrigate, prune for airflow, and remove damaged plant material.

description: Powdery mildew produces superficial fungal growth on cherry foliage and shoots, reducing photosynthesis and fruit development.
causes: The pathogen spreads by airborne conidia and is favored by warm, dry weather with humid nights and shaded dense canopies.
symptoms: White powdery growth on young leaves
Leaf curling and distortion
Stunted shoots
Reduced fruit size or quality
organic_treatment: Improve airflow and apply horticultural oil, sulfur, or potassium bicarbonate products labeled for cherries.
chemical_treatment: Apply a labeled fungicide such as myclobutanil or a strobilurin at early disease stages and rotate modes of action.
prevention: Prune crowded growth, avoid excessive nitrogen, and remove heavily infected shoots from the orchard.

description: Healthy cherry foliage with evenly colored leaves, vigorous shoots, and no visible fungal, bacterial, or viral symptoms.
causes: Balanced orchard nutrition, suitable irrigation, sunlight, and canopy management support healthy cherry growth.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves
Vigorous shoots
Clean leaf margins without spots
Normal blossom and fruit set
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain mulch, irrigation, and routine orchard sanitation.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; use crop protection products only after a confirmed diagnosis.
prevention: Prune for airflow, remove fallen leaves and fruit, and monitor regularly during wet spring conditions.

description: Gray leaf spot is a residue-borne fungal disease that reduces photosynthetic leaf area and can lower corn yield.
causes: Spores develop in infected corn residue and spread during warm, humid periods with prolonged leaf wetness.
symptoms: Rectangular gray or tan lesions between leaf veins
Lesions that expand and merge
Premature loss of lower leaves
Reduced grain fill
organic_treatment: Improve residue decomposition and use resistant hybrids; approved biological or copper products may provide limited protection.
chemical_treatment: Apply a labeled triazole, strobilurin, or premix fungicide when disease threatens the ear leaf before grain fill.
prevention: Rotate crops, manage residue, improve field airflow, and select hybrids with gray-leaf-spot resistance.

description: Citrus greening is a systemic bacterial disease that causes declining trees, mottled leaves, and poor-quality fruit.
causes: The bacterium is spread primarily by the Asian citrus psyllid and through infected grafting material.
symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy leaf mottling
Yellow shoots and vein corking
Small lopsided fruit
Premature fruit drop and tree decline
organic_treatment: There is no curative treatment; remove confirmed infected trees where required and use certified clean replacement stock.
chemical_treatment: Manage psyllid vectors with locally registered insecticides and follow official citrus greening regulatory guidance.
prevention: Use certified nursery material, monitor and control psyllids, and report suspected infections to plant health authorities.

description: Bacterial spot affects peach leaves and fruit, causing defoliation, blemishes, and reduced marketability in warm wet seasons.
causes: Rain splash and wind spread bacteria from infected twigs and leaf lesions; disease is favored by warm weather and frequent wetting.
symptoms: Small angular purple or black leaf spots
Shot-hole appearance after dead tissue drops
Sunken dark fruit lesions
Twig cankers on susceptible trees
organic_treatment: Apply fixed copper products during dormancy and early spring where labeled, and prune infected wood during dry weather.
chemical_treatment: Use labeled oxytetracycline or other registered bactericides and follow peach pre-harvest and resistance-management requirements.
prevention: Choose tolerant cultivars, maintain airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove infected prunings and fruit debris.

description: Healthy peach foliage with consistent green color, active shoot growth, and no visible lesions, curl, or wilt.
causes: Balanced fertility, adequate irrigation, sunlight, and timely orchard sanitation support healthy peach trees.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves
Normal lanceolate leaf shape
Vigorous shoots without cankers
Healthy flowering and fruit development
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain compost, mulch, irrigation, and regular scouting.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; apply products only for a confirmed pest or disease.
prevention: Prune for airflow, remove mummified fruit, and avoid wetting foliage during irrigation.

description: Healthy raspberry foliage with vigorous canes, even green leaves, and no visible lesions, wilt, or nutrient stress.
causes: Well-drained soil, balanced fertility, adequate irrigation, and an open fruiting canopy support healthy raspberry plants.
symptoms: Even green leaf color
Firm productive canes
No cane lesions or leaf spots
Normal flower and berry development
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain organic mulch and balanced fertility.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; use crop protection products only after confirming a specific problem.
prevention: Prune spent canes, maintain row spacing, remove weeds, and use drip irrigation to keep foliage dry.

description: Healthy soybean plants show uniform green trifoliate leaves, strong stems, and normal canopy development without disease lesions.
causes: Effective rhizobial nodulation, balanced fertility, adequate moisture, and suitable field conditions support healthy plants.
symptoms: Uniform green trifoliate leaves
Strong upright stems
No necrotic spots or wilt
Normal flowering and pod set
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain soil health and scout for pests.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; use products only for an identified pest or disease and follow the label.
prevention: Rotate crops, manage weeds, maintain drainage, and scout the canopy regularly during humid weather.

description: Powdery mildew forms white fungal colonies on squash leaves and can reduce photosynthesis, vigor, and fruit production.
causes: Airborne spores infect leaves under warm conditions with high humidity, especially in dense or shaded canopies.
symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves
Yellowing beneath infected colonies
Premature leaf senescence
Reduced fruit size and plant vigor
organic_treatment: Improve airflow and apply potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, or horticultural oil products labeled for squash.
chemical_treatment: Apply a labeled powdery-mildew fungicide such as myclobutanil or a registered strobilurin and rotate modes of action.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties, provide adequate spacing, irrigate at the soil line, and remove severely infected leaves.

description: Strawberry leaf scorch is a fungal foliar disease that produces dark lesions and can reduce plant vigor and fruit yield.
causes: Spores spread by rain splash and irrigation from infected leaves, especially during warm wet periods with dense foliage.
symptoms: Small irregular purple to dark red leaf spots
Spots coalescing into scorched brown patches
Leaf edge necrosis
Reduced plant vigor and fruit production
organic_treatment: Remove infected leaves, improve airflow, and apply labeled copper or biological fungicides during disease-favorable weather.
chemical_treatment: Use a registered strawberry fungicide such as captan or a labeled strobilurin according to local regulations.
prevention: Use clean planting material, avoid overhead irrigation, renew beds appropriately, and remove diseased debris.

description: Healthy strawberry plants have bright green trifoliate leaves, vigorous crowns, and no visible spots, wilt, or rot.
causes: Clean planting stock, well-drained soil, balanced fertility, and appropriate irrigation support healthy strawberry growth.
symptoms: Bright uniform green leaves
Firm crowns and active runners
No leaf lesions or wilt
Normal flowering and fruit development
organic_treatment: No disease treatment is required; maintain clean mulch and balanced organic nutrition.
chemical_treatment: No disease treatment is required; use products only for a confirmed disease or pest.
prevention: Use drip irrigation, provide spacing and airflow, remove old leaves and fruit debris, and rotate beds.

description: Bacterial spot causes leaf and fruit lesions on tomato and can reduce canopy health and marketable yield.
causes: Seedborne or transplantborne bacteria spread through rain splash, overhead irrigation, handling, and wet tools.
symptoms: Small dark water-soaked leaf spots
Yellow halos around lesions
Defoliation under severe pressure
Raised scabby fruit spots
organic_treatment: Remove severely affected tissue and apply labeled fixed copper products with sanitation and dry-canopy management.
chemical_treatment: Use registered copper plus mancozeb programs where permitted and rotate products according to the label.
prevention: Use pathogen-free seed and transplants, avoid overhead irrigation, disinfect tools, and rotate away from solanaceous crops.

description: Septoria leaf spot is a common fungal disease that begins on lower tomato leaves and can cause progressive defoliation.
causes: The fungus survives in infected debris and spreads by rain splash, tools, and wet handling during warm humid weather.
symptoms: Small circular spots with tan centers
Dark margins and tiny black fruiting bodies
Yellowing and drop of lower leaves
Progressive upward defoliation
organic_treatment: Remove infected lower leaves and apply labeled copper or Bacillus products while keeping foliage dry.
chemical_treatment: Apply labeled chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or a registered tomato fungicide before disease becomes severe.
prevention: Mulch to reduce soil splash, stake plants, sanitize debris, rotate crops, and irrigate at the base.

description: Two-spotted spider mites are arthropod pests that damage tomato foliage by extracting cell contents and can rapidly weaken plants.
causes: Populations increase in hot, dry conditions and may flare after broad-spectrum insecticides eliminate natural enemies.
symptoms: Fine pale stippling on leaves
Bronzing or yellowing of foliage
Fine webbing under heavy infestations
Leaf drying and premature drop
organic_treatment: Use strong water sprays, insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or released predatory mites according to labels.
chemical_treatment: Use a registered miticide only when thresholds justify treatment and rotate acaricide modes of action.
prevention: Reduce plant stress, avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides, and scout leaf undersides regularly.

description: Target spot is a fungal disease of tomato foliage and fruit that forms expanding concentric lesions under warm humid conditions.
causes: Spores spread by wind and splashing water from infected debris, with disease favored by extended leaf wetness.
symptoms: Brown circular lesions with concentric rings
Yellowing around leaf spots
Fruit lesions near the stem or shoulders
Premature leaf loss
organic_treatment: Remove infected debris, improve ventilation, and use labeled copper or biological products as preventative protection.
chemical_treatment: Apply a registered tomato fungicide such as chlorothalonil or a labeled strobilurin and rotate modes of action.
prevention: Use crop rotation, stake plants, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove infected plant material promptly.

description: Tomato mosaic virus is a mechanically transmitted virus that causes mottling, distortion, and variable yield loss in tomato plants.
causes: The virus spreads through sap on hands, tools, plant contact, and contaminated seed or plant debris.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic pattern
Leaf narrowing or distortion
Stunting
Uneven fruit ripening or internal browning
organic_treatment: There is no curative treatment; remove infected plants and disinfect tools and hands with an approved sanitizer.
chemical_treatment: No chemical treatment cures the virus; manage weeds and vectors only where they contribute to spread.
prevention: Use certified seed, resistant varieties, strict sanitation, and avoid handling plants while wet.
